title: The Sevapanthis
hook: followers of Bhai Kanhaiya, devoted to quiet service

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nirmala learning, teekas and katha with the line on top, and your line was explained. Today, a stream known less for words than for work.

At the end of a big event, the speakers get the applause and the photos. Then the hall empties, and a few people stay behind. They stack the chairs, wipe the tables, carry the bins out to the curb in the dark. Nobody films that part. In year one you met Bhai Kanhaiya, the water carrier on the battlefield who, the story says, saw his Guru's face in every wounded man. That was one day of his life. Today is about what came after him: people who made the stay-behind part their whole way of life.
screen: `THE SPEAKERS GET THE APPLAUSE.` → `A FEW STAY TO STACK THE CHAIRS.` → `AFTER BHAI KANHAIYA.`

segments.voice: The word is Sevapanthi: one who walks the path of seva, selfless service. Tradition says Bhai Kanhaiya's companions and followers formed a community around his way, and that community still exists. Tradition remembers three things about them. First, service is the center, not a side activity. Sevapanthis are remembered for running places where travelers could rest, drink and eat, and for tending the sick, without asking who anyone was. Second, they lived by their own work. Tradition says they didn't go begging for alms and earned their bread with their hands; serving others while asking nothing of them was the point. Third, quietness: they're remembered less for great deeds with names attached than for steady work over a long time. In Sri Raag, Guru Nanak gives a short line on seva. In paraphrase: do seva in this world, and you will find a place to sit in the Lord's court. Notice where the service happens: in this world, among people, in kitchens and on roads. And notice the reward: not applause, a seat, the way a tired traveler finds one at a Sevapanthi rest stop. Some Sikhs hear echoes of this in the langar, and in the shoe room at the gurdwara, where volunteers polish strangers' shoes. The Sevapanthis took that common Sikh practice and made it the name of their path. Not service as a break from real life; service as the real life, with the rest fitted in around it.
screen: `SEVAPANTHI: THE PATH OF SEVA.` · `REST, WATER AND FOOD FOR ANYONE.` · `BREAD EARNED BY THEIR OWN HANDS.` · `SRI RAAG: SERVE HERE, A SEAT THERE.` · then, large: `SERVICE FIRST.`

segments.voice: Think of one small job in the hours ahead that nobody will thank you for, a dish in the sink, a shared space to tidy, and picture yourself doing it quietly and walking away without mentioning it. Breathe out the wish to be seen, and if you pray, rest on Waheguru.
Sevapanthi. One on the path of seva: a community that, tradition says, follows Bhai Kanhaiya, living by its own work and serving anyone. Today's word.
Your line: service first. The seat comes without the applause, and that is enough. Until tomorrow.

chat.says: What made the Sevapanthis different? Don't all Sikhs do seva?
options: Many do. Sevapanthis made seva the center, living by their own work and asking nothing back.
They did seva only on festival days, and rested from it the rest of the year.
They served only fellow Sikhs, and asked travelers who they were first.
chat.meaning: Tradition remembers the Sevapanthis for serving anyone, travelers and the sick, while earning their bread by their own hands.
